props.title: Multiple Maniacs

sections.content: **Multiple Maniacs** (1970) marks John Waters' first feature-length assault on good taste, paving the way for his signature shock cinema. Shot in grainy 16mm for $5,000 in Baltimore, this transgressive masterpiece follows Divine as Lady Divine, who runs a traveling freak show called The Cavalcade of Perversion before descending into murderous madness. The film established Waters' core ensemble including David Lochary, Mink Stole, and Cookie Mueller, while pushing boundaries with its gleefully blasphemous "Rosary Job" scene and surreal giant lobster rape finale. Waters cites influences from the Manson murders and underground films like **Flaming Creatures** (1963), creating his own distinct brand of trash cinema.

sections.content: Waters' early shock films emerged from a vibrant 1960s-70s underground cinema scene. While **Multiple Maniacs** drew inspiration from exploitation pioneers like Herschell Gordon Lewis' **Blood Feast** (1963), it also paralleled experimental works like the Kuchar brothers' **Hold Me While I'm Naked** (1966) and Paul Morrissey's **Flesh** (1968). The DIY aesthetic, transgressive content, and blurring of high/low art aligned with the emerging midnight movie phenomenon that would later embrace **El Topo** (1970) and **Pink Flamingos** (1972).

The film's raw energy and guerrilla filmmaking approach influenced later underground auteurs. You can trace its DNA through the Cinema of Transgression movement, particularly films like **They Eat Scum** (1979) and Nick Zedd's works. Waters refined this crude template in subsequent features, but **Multiple Maniacs** remains his most unhinged vision - a perfect crystallization of his early "trash trilogy" period before reaching wider audiences with **Polyester** (1981) and **Hairspray** (1988). movies.slug: Waters goes mainstream-adjacent with Divine as a suburban housewife whose life unravels, featuring scratch-and-sniff "Odorama" cards

sections.content: Divine's ferocious performance as Lady Divine set the template for their future collaborations. Unlike later, more polished roles in **Hairspray** (1988) or **Lust in the Dust** (1985), here Divine channels raw, unrestrained energy that borders on genuine menace. The character's descent into homicidal mania predates similar exploitation film narratives like **Ms. 45** (1981) or **They Call Her One Eye** (1973), while maintaining Waters' signature black humor.
